title: Rethinking "RL Generalizes, SFT Memorizes": The Role of SFT Data
authors: Yunlong Hou, Fengzhuo Zhang, Yuan Cheng et al.
abstract: Large language models trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) with verifiable rewards exhibit strong reasoning ability and broad generalization, whereas models trained with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) are often viewed as more prone to memorization and limited transfer. This paper rethinks this distinction through the lens of SFT training data on widely used Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 series models. title: MLIRBench - A Benchmark and Dataset for Compiler and Hardware-Aware Reasoning
authors: Pranava Sai Maganti, Meghasyam Peddireddy, Muzakker Hossain et al.
abstract: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly popular in software engineering and have performed well on different programming tasks. However, it is still difficult to know whether these models truly understand program behavior or whether they mainly rely on patterns learned from their training data. title: NIBench: benchmarking autonomous AI agents for execution, skill evolution and scientific judgment in neuroimaging
authors: Lujia Zhong, Yihao Xia, Jianwei Zhang et al.
abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly used to automate biomedical research, creating a growing need to benchmark their capabilities on real scientific data and workflows. Their reliability in neuroimaging remains insufficiently characterized, where plausible analytical outputs can conceal errors that affect scientific conclusions. title: Fine-Grained Generative Hallucination Detection and Correction for Aerial Image Captioning
authors: Debolena Basak, Somsubhra De, Maunendra Sankar Desarkar
abstract: Aerial imagery captured by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) plays a vital role in applications such as surveillance, disaster response, and large-scale environmental monitoring. Automatic generation of textual descriptions for such imagery is essential for reducing manual inspection overhead and enabling better downstream decision-making. title: VibePrevisBench: Evaluating Agentic Coding for 4D Scene Generation in Blender
authors: Yuzhe Chen, Muxi Diao, Lele Yang et al.
abstract: Controllable real-world video generation models can condition on a rendered graybox proxy video, which fixes layout, motion and camera. Coding agents can build such videos by reconstructing a 4D scene in Blender, yet no benchmark checks both these videos and the long, multi-shot scenes behind them. We introduce VibePrevisBench, a benchmark for 4D scene reconstruction: an agent turns a brief into an executable 4D scene and renders its proxy video. title: TraceKV: Policy-Preserving Low-Rank KV Cache Compression for Reasoning Vision-Language Models
authors: Ke Li, Zishan Shao, Yiran Chen
abstract: Reasoning vision-language models (VLMs) impose substantial KV cache demands from both large multimodal contexts and growing reasoning traces. Low-rank KV compression has emerged as a promising paradigm that stores low-dimensional latents of KV states and can be combined with quantization. However, existing low-rank methods often induce growing predictive policy drift from the dense model when compressing reasoning KV states, resulting in reasoning failures. title: AROMA: Adaptive Representation-Oriented Multimodal Actuation for Vision-Language Model Control
authors: Zhaoning Zhang
abstract: Mechanistic localization does not by itself yield usable control: causal sensitivity may occupy little activation energy, an accurate local direction may fail at finite scale, and a reachable numeral target may be wrong. We introduce AROMA (Adaptive Representation-Oriented Multimodal Actuation), a frozen-VLM control framework separating where to intervene, which geometry and gain to use, how to reach a target, which target to pursue, and when to act. title: Emergent Vision-Shaped Thinking in Text-Only Reasoning through Multimodal Training
authors: Qi Zhang, Bohan Wang, Qianru Sun et al.
abstract: Does multimodal training shape how a language model thinks, even when the input is text only? We test this with targeted causal ablations across 10 multimodal configurations from 6 model families, with matched text-only backbones and cross-family transfer controls. We contrast spatial-imagery tasks that invite mental scene construction with symbol-manipulation tasks solvable by symbolic rules alone. We identify a vision-language axis in hidden-state space and ablate its projection at inference.

title: Learning a calibrated decision head from logged bandit feedback
authors: Ye Yuan
abstract: A decision head reads a state and a list of options and returns a probability per option in one forward pass. Once deployed, it usually observes only whether the option it chose was right: logged bandit feedback. We adapt such a head, LoRA on Qwen3-0.6B-Base and 1.7B-Base, from that feedback and report three results. title: Can We Make an LLM Dumber, or Is It Just Playing Dumb? An Empirical Study of Believable Performance Throttling
authors: Chengguang Gan, Yunhao Liang, Hanjun Wei et al.
abstract: A benchmark score is commonly read as a proxy for model capability. We study the inverse problem: can a model be driven to a target score, and do its failures resemble those of a naturally weaker model? We operationalize believable performance reduction along three axes: target calibration, item-difficulty structure, and error-distribution similarity to a real weak reference. title: Scaling public input on AI policy with pluralistic agents
authors: Jacy Reese Anthis, Ken Burke, David Madras et al.
abstract: AI is being deployed across a vast range of application domains, cultural environments, and human stakeholders. Safe and responsible AI development requires continuously accounting for diverse perspectives. We develop and test pluralistic agents, AI agent representatives that deliberate on behalf of individuals to align AI systems with diverse human perspectives. Pluralistic agents could help people contribute to many more discussions than they could directly participate in, on technical topics

title: HeriKGQA: Grounded Knowledge-Graph Question Answering over Cultural Heritage Sensor Data
authors: Lingxiao Kong, Vasileios Arampatzakis, Vasileios Sevetlidis et al.
abstract: Cultural heritage sites are increasingly monitored by sensor networks, but querying their data requires database expertise. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a natural-language interface, yet over raw sensor records they lose track of which sensor, site, and time each value belongs to, and silently miscompute. title: Speech Tokenizers are Vulnerable: Transferable Semantic Attack and Robust Tokenizer
authors: Zhisheng Zhang, Yifan Mi, Yixuan Zhou et al.
abstract: Speech tokenizers serve as speech front ends, encoding input speech signals into representations for downstream models, such as automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems and large audio-language models (LALMs). In this paper, we find that speech tokenizers are fragile at the semantic level: small perturbations can disrupt their semantic encoding process and consequently cause severe degradation in downstream ASR and LALM performance. title: Subsurface schematisation from sparse CPT data using the tabular foundation model TabPFN
authors: Taiga Saito, Fabian Campos Montero, Bruno Zuada Coelho et al.
abstract: Subsurface schematisation supports geotechnical decisions but remains challenging because sparse site-investigation data leave substantial gaps in information about ground conditions. This study explores TabPFN, a foundation model pretrained on general synthetic tabular data, for this task. title: What Roles Do System Prompts Really Assign? Validating and Steering Occupational Role Vectors in LLMs
authors: Jose L. Sampedro Mazon, Ilmi Yoon, Nadim Saad
abstract: Applications built on large language models assign the model a role through its system prompt, intending to shape how it responds for their use case. We introduce a validation framework for extracting and injecting occupational role vectors, activation-level directions that capture how someone in a given occupational role would distinctively respond to a task or question. title: DuoJEPA: Cross-Modal Translation Between Unaligned Self-Supervised Embedding Spaces
authors: Mahmut S. Gokmen, Mitchell A. Klusty, Evan W. Damron et al.
abstract: Learning from paired modalities is commonly equated with aligning them: two encoders are trained until the embeddings of a pair coincide in a shared space. We study whether cross-modal retrieval and classification can instead be obtained while the two encoders' own embedding spaces remain directly unaligned. title: Large Payments Model
authors: Natraj Raman, Abhenandhan Manoharan, Vishwasreddy Thuniki et al.
abstract: Payment applications such as fraud detection, authorization prediction, and payment optimization draw on overlapping transaction information. This motivates a reusable payments intelligence layer that shares learned representations and predictive signals, rather than developing predictive models independently for each task. title: Where Is Uncertainty Observed? A Mechanistic Understanding of Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs
authors: Xiaoyu Liang, Virginia Ceccatelli, Aliai Eusebi et al.
abstract: Knowing when a large language model's (LLM's) response can be trusted is critical for its safe use. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) can help LLMs recognize if their responses may be unreliable. Existing taxonomies organize UQ methods by uncertainty source or estimation mechanism. They leave unresolved the question of where uncertainty is observed in the model's computation. title: Curiosity-0826-4B: Generative Medical Event Sequence Modeling Across Pediatric and Adult Populations
authors: Mani Nagarathnam, Luke Benham, Paul Blazek et al.
abstract: We introduce Curiosity-0826-4B, an updated version of the generative medical event foundation model trained on Epic Cosmos that simulates patient timelines to produce zero-shot clinical predictions. Curiosity-0826-4B incorporates a broader patient population and richer clinical event representations, while generally matching or exceeding Curiosity-0226-1B, the largest model in the previous Curiosity-0226 series, on evaluated tasks supported by both models. title: TopoST: Topology-Conditioned Node Specialization for Urban Spatio-Temporal Foundation Models
authors: Kaiyun Wei, Yue Xu, Wenying Duan et al.
abstract: Urban spatio-temporal foundation models must share knowledge across diverse urban scenarios while accommodating heterogeneous node dynamics. Our analysis of 20+ datasets spanning diverse urban scenarios reveals recurring local graph structures across datasets alongside substantial node heterogeneity within local subgraphs. title: Is the Importance Ratio Necessary for Stable Reinforcement Learning in LLMs?
authors: Shuibai Zhang, Junhyuck Kim, Gyeongman Kim et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become central to post-training large language models (LLMs). However, popular RL methods like GRPO incur non-negligible overhead by computing both old-policy and current-policy likelihoods to form importance sampling ratios. In this work, we propose Likelihood-Gated Policy Optimization (LGPO), which enforces a soft trust region constraint via likelihood-based gating, eliminating the need to compute old-policy likelihoods. title: Multi-head Quantum Neural Networks: Replacing Transformer Blocks with NISQ Modules inside a 30-Billion-Parameter LLM
authors: Maforikan Amoussou, Borja Aizpurua, Sukhbinder Singh et al.
abstract: We introduce the multi-head quantum neural network (QNN), a quantum module compatible with noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices that can replace transformer blocks inside pre-trained large language models (LLMs) with little loss in accuracy and with far fewer parameters than the blocks it replaces. title: Where is My Mug? Training-Free Framework for Personalized Image Segmentation
authors: Quang Qui-Vinh Nguyen, Hung Nguyen, Rang Nguyen et al.
abstract: \textbf{Personalized Image Segmentation (PIS)} aims to segment the specific object in a target image that matches a user-provided reference. Unlike category-based segmentation or few-shot segmentation, PIS must discriminate between multiple visually similar instances, a requirement central to deployed applications such as augmented reality, personalized content editing, robotics manipulation, inventory tracking, and fine-grained visual retrieval. title: FIBER: Bayesian Fusion of Fast-DetectGPT and IRT-Informed Detector Evidence for LLM-Generated Text Detection
authors: Yan Li, Guangsheng Bao, Zhipeng Chen et al.
abstract: Detecting large language model (LLM)-generated text remains challenging under domain and generator shifts. Supervised detectors may generalize poorly, while zero-shot methods often rely on individual statistical signals without leveraging historical detector behavior. We propose FIBER (Fast-DetectGPT with IRT-informed Bayesian Evidence Recalibration), which integrates continuous Fast-DetectGPT scores with auxiliary detector outputs through Bayesian evidence fusion. title: A Time-Frequency-Condition Multimodal Fusion Foundation Model for Universal Rotating-Machinery Fault Diagnosis under Multi-Element Heterogeneous Scenarios
authors: Xinyu Zou, Jian Ma, Liang Ma et al.
abstract: Intelligent fault diagnosis models are typically developed for a single machine under a specific set of operating conditions, such that each new machine or condition requires retraining from scratch. This one-machine-one-model paradigm scales poorly. Although transfer learning and domain generalization can reduce the labeling burden, they primarily seek domain-invariant commonality, potentially discarding machine-specific characteristics that are critical for diagnosis. title: Prototypes of the Mind: A Unified Framework for Probing the Visual Brain
authors: Shi Chen, Seoyoung Ahn, Doris Tsao
abstract: Deep learning has driven substantial progress in modeling fMRI responses, yet most existing approaches are optimized for a single objective---such as neural encoding, stimulus decoding, or post hoc interpretation---making it difficult to obtain a coherent account of neural representations. We introduce a unified framework that connects vision foundation models to brain activity while supporting neural analysis from multiple complementary perspectives. title: A Cardiorespiratory Foundation Model Pretrained on Ten Physiological Signals for Perioperative and Critical Care
authors: Cheol-Hui Lee, Wookyung Kim, Hyeonhoon Lee et al.
abstract: Arterial, venous, pulmonary artery and intracranial pressures and ventilator waveforms guide decisions in operating rooms and intensive care units, yet foundation models for physiological waveforms have been built almost entirely on the electrocardiogram and photoplethysmogram. We present CARMEN, a single encoder pretrained without labels on ten cardiorespiratory waveforms (2.27 million modality-hours). title: MuEdit: An efficient multi-task editing method towards inter-domain knowledge conflicts
authors: Songshi Liang, Ting-En Lin, Zixuan Huang et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require frequent knowledge updates across heterogeneous domains, but existing editing methods fail when applied sequentially to multi-task settings. We trace this collapse to inter-domain null-space misalignment: heterogeneous tasks induce distinct Jacobian geometries, causing their common null space to shrink dramatically and leaving insufficient admissible directions for conflict-free updates. title: Hy ASR 3.0 Technical Report
authors: Aoxiong Yin, Auden Li, Chao Huang et al.
abstract: We present Hy ASR 3.0, a large language model (LLM)-based automatic speech recognition (ASR) system that delivers strong recognition accuracy, supports flexible contextual conditioning, and maintains robust recognition performance across diverse speech conditions. Hy ASR 3.0 supports Mandarin Chinese, English and 13 Chinese dialect groups, including Cantonese. title: Is Jev a Good Multilingual Judge?
authors: Wei Liu, Yi Fan, Xiyan Fu
abstract: Generative large language models are widely used for multilingual text evaluation, yet whether decision models that directly output judgment probabilities can serve as multilingual judges has received limited attention. We evaluate Jev against generative LLM judges on four multilingual benchmarks with human annotations, covering up to 47 language varieties and three evaluation formats: binary decisions, pairwise comparisons, and graded ratings. title: Video-as-Experience: Learning Computer Use via Audio-Visual Understanding
authors: Guangzhi Sun, Zhonghao Zhai, Yixuan Li et al.
abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) have enabled capable computer-use agents that perceive graphical user interfaces, reason over instructions, and execute actions. However, existing approaches to learning from video demonstrations typically convert videos into screenshot-based action trajectories, rather than directly leveraging their rich audio-visual information. title: TETHER: Training-Free, Elastic, ToC-Anchored Hierarchy Extraction and Recovery in Design-Driven Long Documents
authors: Yu Zou, Yan Chen, Jialei Zeng et al.
abstract: Converting complex documents into structured knowledge constitutes the critical infrastructure urgently required for deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in downstream research. title: Controlled Knowledge Engineering for Taxonomy Induction with Tool-Grounded LLM Agents and Runtime-Adaptive Policies
authors: Jonas Limniatis, Bennet Schaarmann, Georg Reuber et al.
abstract: Taxonomies are structured knowledge representations that support semantic search, recommendation, product catalog organization, and retrieval-augmented generation. Their automated construction from a fixed set of candidate entities requires more than plausible text generation: the resulting hierarchy must be complete, structurally valid, and semantically coherent. title: OpticalRAG: Pixel-Space Compression for Token-Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Senhao Liu, Yuheng Zhang, Chunyu Wei et al.
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is bottlenecked by the token budget of large language models: feeding long documents into the context window is expensive, while aggressive textual compression discards fine-grained information that is irreversibly lost in a one-dimensional token sequence. We argue that this bottleneck is not fundamental to information density but to the choice of compression \emph{modality}. title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
authors: Ruiheng Yu, Oteo Mamo, Siyu Gan et al.
abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are enabling software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers to automate longer business workflows with agents. In subscription-based SaaS deployments, model and tool calls consume provider resources without additional customer payments. Because the agent autonomously decides when to stop, a malicious tenant can send a prompt to the agent, exploiting its completion decisions to extend execution and waste provider resources. title: Mach2: Scientific Discovery Platform with Deterministic Execution Constraints
authors: Vansh Sharma, Venkat Raman
abstract: Language-model agents can formulate workflows and invoke specialized tools, yet compliance with natural-language operating rules is not guaranteed by prompting alone. Mach2 addresses this limitation by coupling Eigen orchestration to deterministic, lint-like checks of tool requests, source changes, acceptance tests, and artifact contracts. title: Cleaning an Agent's History Hurts When the World Still Holds the Error
authors: Egor Pakhomov, Anurag Koul, Hongjun Liu et al.
abstract: Tool-using language-model agents accumulate histories of their own mistakes, and a system that compacts, repairs or hands off such a history decides what it says about those mistakes while their effects stay in the world. Prior work cleans the history at a fixed world, where showing a corrected step and saying it is done move together. title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
authors: Ziang Liu, James J. Kim, Yijia Dai et al.
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows
authors: Kaiyuan Hou, Yang Ping Kuo, Indranil Bhattacharya et al.
abstract: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. title: KernelMosaic: An Open Dataset and Agentic Framework for CUDA Kernel Generation
authors: Ningyuan Xi, Yuhang Lai, Ning Miao
abstract: Training large language models to generate efficient CUDA kernels requires supervision spanning diverse computational requirements and iterative code optimization. Constructing this supervision is challenging because of heterogeneous specifications, and useful implementations emerge through iterative complicated testing and refinement. We introduce KernelMosaic, an open dataset pairing diverse CUDA tasks with verified solutions and trajectories. Human-guided review and diversity-aware selection

title: When Should Agents Remember? Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution for LLM Agents
authors: Runxuan Tang, Haoyu Gao, Yuyan Ding et al.
abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon, verifier-rich environments, but current self-improvement mechanisms often write episode-derived lessons directly into memory, making local success an unreliable signal for reusable and safe knowledge. This paper addresses the core question of when an experience-derived behavioral update should be admitted into persistent agent state. title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
authors: Yukyeong Lee, Yumin Choi, Jinheon Baek et al.
abstract: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. title: Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class: A Policed Quality-of-Service Mechanism for Agentic AI Traffic, Evaluated from Simulation to Real-Kernel Adversarial Testing
authors: Naveen Babu Narayanan Nair, Sajay Kurup
abstract: Software agents built on large language models generate traffic unlike human web traffic, yet routers have no class for it and cannot verify a sender's claim to be an agent. This paper proposes the Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class (VATC), which combines a reserved Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) value declaring agent traffic, a router-side classifier that demotes flows contradicting the declaration to a class served after best-effort traffic, and a rate-limited priority queue. title: Looking One Step Ahead: An Anticipation-guided Agent for Object State Readout in Videos
authors: Yuanhe Tian, Yan Song
abstract: Understanding the progress of an activity requires tracking how the objects involved change over time. Object state readout provides this information by describing a target object's states and transitions across video frames. Although multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate detailed visual descriptions, these descriptions may leave the attributes needed to distinguish successive states insufficiently specified. title: Program-Aided Patchable Skill Evolution
authors: Jiahao Wang, Yuqi Xiong, Qing Yang et al.
abstract: Agent skills have emerged as an effective means of enabling LLM agents to solve complex, interactive tasks by encoding reusable knowledge without modifying model parameters. Recent approaches further improve skill adaptation by distilling reusable experience from agent execution trajectories and evolving skills based on downstream task feedback. authors: Lirui Luo, Kelong Mao, Xinwei Yang et al.
abstract: Language-model agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks whose interaction histories exceed the model's active context. They must therefore decide what to write down and what to read back, and when to do either. Recent work has begun to use on-policy distillation (OPD) to make memory control part of the policy, relying on memory tools and compaction protocols that lie outside either model's pre-training. title: TreeAgent: Structure-Aware Memory Agent for Processing Long Hierarchical Data
authors: Wei Gu, Weiwei Qi, Jiajun Tang et al.
abstract: Practical Web applications increasingly require agents to interpret long conversations or documents. For inputs exceeding the context windows of large language models (LLMs), memory agents process segments sequentially and retain past information in bounded memory. title: Toward Autonomous RTL and Synthesis Optimization: Benchmarking and Self-Improving Agents
authors: Wenji Fang, Yao Lu, Jinghua Wang et al.
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents are creating new opportunities for hardware design optimization. This paper examines three connected directions toward autonomous RTL and synthesis optimization: (1) Realistic benchmarking. authors: Burak Susam, Ruiyuan Kang, Tingting Mu
abstract: Manifold embedding for data visualisation is dominated by a small set of hand-designed state-of-the-art (SOTA) algorithms. Their design targets are fixed at development time, resulting in inflexible algorithmic behaviour that cannot be readily steered towards user-specified structural priorities. Hand-designing new embedding algorithms to address user priority requires highly specialised expertise and is time consuming. title: On Private Knowledge Retrieval and Private Inference for secure multi-agent systems
authors: Vicenç Torra, Maria Bras-Amorós
abstract: Multi-agent systems provide a convenient framework for the massive deployment of agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs). It provides a sound framework where agents can interact with existing software to perform actions in an autonomous way. Agentic AI is the new term to denote these AI-based autonomous systems. title: DrugCoding: A Scientific Programming Agent for Drug Discovery
authors: Junwei Hu, Zhuohao Lin, Kun Li et al.
abstract: Drug discovery involves multiple interconnected research stages, including molecular design, property prediction, and virtual screening. These processes are characterized by complex workflows, interdependent computational tasks, and diverse specialized tools, placing substantial demands on the coordination of scientific models and computational resources. title: Synapse-Control: Making Agent Experience Actionable with Lightweight Runtime Control
authors: Zhiyuan Huang, Shengan Zheng, Chenghu Yang et al.
abstract: Large language model agents reuse execution experience to improve reliability on complex tool-based tasks. Systems such as Sentry call large models to generate failure diagnoses before retrieving advice, adding inference cost to experience reuse. authors: Sungbin Im
abstract: Agentic workflows, in which a large language model (LLM) calls tools to read and write data, are evaluated in two ways. Benchmarks compare the final state against a gold answer. Deployed services have none; an LLM judge reads the transcript and decides. Practice treats the two as interchangeable. This paper measures whether they are. authors: Mingchen Li, Yongkang Xiao, Rumeng Li et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential in biomedical applications, while agentic memory systems have emerged as a promising approach to preserving and utilizing information across tasks and interactions. However, a fundamental question remains: how effectively and reliably do these systems retain, retrieve, update, and utilize biomedical information? title: Bursts That Outlast Themselves: Persistent Degradation in Prefix-Cached Agent Serving
authors: Wen Huang, Jack Liu
abstract: LLM agents drive inference engines with closed-loop sessions whose context grows every turn, and serving them economically depends on prefix caching: a hit costs an incremental prefill of about a thousand tokens, a miss recomputes a 10--40K-token context. We show that this makes prefix-cached agent serving metastable. authors: Genming Cui, Xiangyu Li, Zixu Hao et al.
abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the inference cost of LLM agents but can compromise task success. Examining failed rollouts, we find that quantized agents overlook task requirements or environmental conditions, producing environment transitions that diverge from successful full-precision references. title: Stinging the Swarm: Extracting Attacker Intelligence from a Twin-Controller OT Honeypot
authors: Canyon Grey Dell'Omo, Joao Pedro de Carvalho Voltani
abstract: Autonomous language-model agents can drive industrial controllers over fieldbus protocols, probing a plant at machine speed and in coordinated swarms. We present Talos, an inline gate that judges every agent request to a controller in milliseconds and routes agents it flags as hostile to a device-faithful decoy -- a mirror twin of the real plant -- where their attack continues harmlessly and is read for intelligence. authors: Nhi Nguyen, Shauli Ravfogel, Rajesh Ranganath
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly make consequential decisions and solve problems alongside humans, we must understand how models arrive at their conclusions. Understanding how an LLM behaves requires observing it across multiple inputs, yet free-text explanations such as chain-of-thought (CoT) are generated per instance and cannot be easily verified on new inputs. title: Cognitive Mapping of Learning by Thinking Mechanisms in Large Language Models
authors: Dong Han, Jin Zhang, Kunyue Yang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly exhibit capabilities that resemble human Learning by Thinking (LbT), the acquisition of new insight through internal processes such as explanation and reasoning, without new external input. title: Breakdown of Autoregressive Multi-Step Reasoning Under Concentrated vs. Diffuse Attention Head Dropout
authors: Karol Struniawski
abstract: During extended wakefulness, mammalian neocortical networks experience localized periods of transient neuronal silence termed off-states. Here, we examine how analogous spatiotemporally concentrated disruptions affect sequential reasoning in autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs). title: Hx2Dx: From Anamnesis to Diagnosis - A Multimodal Arena for Conversational Clinical Reasoning in LLMs
authors: Federico Ravenda, Mirko Cesarini, Daniele Montagnani et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve expert-level diagnostic accuracy in static evaluations, where the model receives a curated vignette or case report that already condenses the diagnostically relevant findings. Such evaluations measure inference over already selected evidence; the evaluations do not account for the inquiry used to obtain it. title: ProofCoder: Continuous Reasoning for Automated Software Verification
authors: Martim Afonso, Inês Lynce, Maurizio Morisio et al.
abstract: Formal verification using proof assistants provides strong correctness guarantees for software, but constructing proofs remains labor-intensive and requires significant expertise. Recent approaches based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating proof synthesis. title: Interleaving anatomical inspection and diagnostic reasoning for explainable radiology report generation
authors: Chentao Huang, Runlong Lin, Zhijun Wang et al.
abstract: Automated radiology report generation can draft clinically plausible reports, yet the pathway from visual evidence to reported findings remains opaque, leaving the diagnostic basis of these reports unexplained and the generated reports difficult to review or revise. title: Transparency Disclosures for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
authors: Jacob Davies, Theo Bearman
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is one of the most valuable tools for monitoring advanced AI systems, but it is under threat. We argue that frontier AI developers should report specific indicators to make these threats trackable and to better facilitate coordination to preserve CoT monitorability. authors: Bastien Dussard, Aur{é}lie Clodic, Guillaume Sarthou
abstract: While symbolic reasoning for task allocation requires grounding a robot's physical capabilities, standard Unified Robot Description Format (URDF) files provide only low-level kinematics without the formal semantic context needed for reasoning. We present URDF2Ontology, an automated, taxonomy-agnostic neurosymbolic framework that transforms raw URDF files into populated, grounded OWL ontologies. title: Transformers Provably Learn Graph Search: Training Dynamics and the Exponential Power of Depth
authors: Xutao Ma, Somayeh Sojoudi
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress on complex reasoning tasks, yet the mechanisms by which they acquire reasoning capabilities and the efficiency of their reasoning remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the path-finding problem over directed graphs, a symbolic abstraction of multi-step reasoning. authors: Niall Dalton
abstract: Post-training improves language-model reasoning, but how it changes the use of internal information and verbalized chain of thought (CoT) remains unclear. We study successive SFT, DPO, and RLVR checkpoints of Olmo-3-7B-Instruct on multi-digit addition, using carry values as known intermediate state. title: Reasoning-Aware Relational Representation Learning for Open-Vocabulary Scene Graph Generation
authors: Jiawei Xiao, Boya Wang, Longtian Qiu et al.
abstract: Open-Vocabulary Scene Graph Generation (OV-SGG) requires models to recognize visual relationships beyond the training vocabulary, yet existing methods often rely on dataset-specific object--predicate co-occurrence patterns. Under long-tailed distributions and noisy object localization, such reliance leads to biased, entangled relation representations, limiting both rare-relation recognition and generalization to unseen predicates. authors: Oliver Lack, Lana Tikhomirov, Humphrey Thompson et al.
abstract: As AI-based products permeate society, specifically systems using generative models, a belief system is emerging about what these products are and what they can and cannot do. One common belief concerns the perception of the form of language as evidence of 'understanding' language. title: An LLM Is All You Need: Data-Efficient Adaptation to Full-Duplex, Word-Level Spoken Dialogue
authors: Tairan Chen, Richard Yucheng He, Yihang Liu et al.
abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue, in which a system listens while it speaks and can backchannel, yield the floor, and be interrupted, is usually obtained by training on hundreds of thousands to millions of hours of speech. This is costly, rewrites the language model that supplies the system's knowledge, and still leaves turn-taking either implicit or decided coarsely rather than word by word. authors: Matteo Gabburo, Daniela Baiamonte, Stefano Simonazzi et al.
abstract: Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) perform strongly on multimodal tasks, Document Understanding (DU) among them, but the benchmarks that measure them mostly cover English documents and narrow problems. How well current VLMs generalize across languages, tasks, styles and layouts therefore remains unclear. authors: Eoin M. Kenny, Salim I. Amoukou, Tom Bewley
abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) has expanded into a broad and impactful research area, but the fundamental question of how best to evaluate explanation techniques has proven frustratingly elusive. Methodologies typically revolve around either proxy metrics which tell us little about the utility of an explanation, or human evaluation which---while generally considered the gold standard---is expensive, difficult to scale, and challenging to reproduce. title: DisasterAgent: An Evidence-Driven Agent for Verifiable Disaster Report Generation From Remote Sensing Imagery
authors: Zhijian Li, Jiawei Song, Chao Ren et al.
abstract: Remote sensing disaster assessment is moving from simple damage classification toward comprehensive report-level analysis. In this setting, responders need not only damage descriptions but also verifiable evidence to guide response and recovery. authors: Qinan Zhang, Xinyu Wang, Qihang Jin et al.
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for multimodal and embodied tasks, yet aggregate accuracy or consistency alone does not reveal whether a judge changes its verdict for the right reason. authors: Mikhail Kulakov, Ruslan Solikhov, Ivan Bondarenko
abstract: We present our system for the SHROOM-visions 2026 shared task on character-level hallucination span detection in image-conditioned vision-language model (VLM) responses, evaluated across English, French, Italian, and Chinese. title: HandsOnAid: Building and Evaluating an Offline First-Aid Assistant for Emergency Response Scenarios
authors: Rezwan Islam Salvi, Saiyma Sittul Muna, Mushfiqur Rahman Mushfique
abstract: Emergencies can occur where there is no phone signal and no ambulance nearby. A small language model on a phone can be helpful in such situations, but its advice needs to be safe and accurate. We built HandsOnAid, a 4-bit Gemma 2B model fine-tuned with QLoRA on FirstAidQA dataset, a corpus of 5,550 first-aid question-answer pairs. authors: Chi Liu, Xin Chen, Yuchuan Weng et al.
abstract: In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, a language model is rewarded for a correct final answer, and GRPO passes that reward to every token of the solution in equal measure. authors: Chaeho Lee, Junyup Kim, Wansoo Kim et al.
abstract: Integrating human feedback into language models has gained increasing attention as a means to align model outputs with human preferences, with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) serving as a prominent framework for preference-based alignment. title: Specify Privacy Yourself: Assessing Inference-Time Personalized Privacy Preservation Ability of Large Vision-Language Models
authors: Xingqi Wang, Xiaoyuan Yi, Xing Xie et al.
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities but raise significant privacy concerns due to their abilities to infer sensitive personal information from images with high precision. While current LVLMs are relatively well aligned to protect universal privacy, e.g., credit card data, we argue that privacy is inherently personalized and context-dependent. authors: Yuka Saito, Ikumi Numaya, Jun Suzuki et al.
abstract: As large language models generate increasingly high-quality responses, recent work on response evaluation has moved beyond response-centered criteria, such as correctness and coherence, toward user-centered criteria, including user preferences and perceived usefulness. abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language models by distilling teacher predictions on student-generated trajectories, while on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) removes the need for an external teacher by using a reference-conditioned copy of the model as the teacher. authors: Aghoghomena Akasukpe, Li Yang, Xinyao Zhou et al.
abstract: Verifying corporate financial disclosures against the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) is a core auditing task in which experts cross-reference disclosures with hundreds of fine-grained regulatory paragraphs: a laborious, costly, and error-prone process that motivates growing interest in large language models (LLMs) as compliance assistants. authors: Haoyi Wu, Yunkai Dang, Wanyu Zhang et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across diverse applications, making both safety and utility essential for reliable deployment. authors: Paulo Camara
abstract: Most language models deployed outside the United States and China are fine-tuned descendants of a small number of pretrained families. authors: Zhikun Tao, Fangyong Jin, Junping Zhao
abstract: Reusing key--value (KV) caches across language model updates could avoid repeated computation of shared context, but changes in model weights raise a fundamental question about what these caches preserve. authors: Riya Naik, Shivam Sharma, Swati Agarwal
abstract: India's temples and other places of worship are among its richest repositories of cultural heritage, bringing together religious tradition, history, architecture, and art. Due to the widespread curiosity, people increasingly turn to Artificial Intelligence (AI) assistants for information about them. Current models are rarely trained or evaluated on this domain. abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems have demonstrated remarkable effectiveness in mitigating hallucinations by incorporating external knowledge. abstract: Accurate, compact exchange--correlation functionals are central to predictive density functional theory. authors: Shaohuang Wang, Jinghao Wen, Xulei Zhang et al.
abstract: When an LLM agent fails part-way through a long task, the usual analysis records a symptom: a failure-mode label, or the agent and step judged responsible. authors: Rayed AlGhamdi
abstract: This study examines the reliability of Claude Code, an agentic deployment of the Claude Opus 4.6 large language model, as a grading system for handwritten university exams. authors: Dipin Khati, Shubham Mehrotra, Bin Bi et al.
abstract: Domain-specific languages (DSLs) are widely used in enterprise software, giving a compact interface to complex tasks, from data access to infrastructure automation. Platforms increasingly extend them to agents, where a developer declares the topics, permitted actions, and guardrails of an agent rather than writing general-purpose code. authors: Sepideh Ravanbakhsh, Hamidreza Moradi
abstract: Effective search and rescue (SAR) operations require autonomous systems capable of coordinating multiple heterogeneous agents, adapting to dynamic hazards, and aligning with human mission intent. authors: Chang Liu, Bo Wu
abstract: Effective teaching requires reasoning about the learner as well as the task, a capacity that Theory of Mind describes as inferring another agent's latent state from its behavior. We ask whether a stronger LLM teaches a fixed student better when it applies this principle. authors: Jeheon Woo
abstract: Coding agents built on large language models, run in automated improvement loops, can discover more efficient algorithms. authors: Erik Derner, Jiří Kubalík, Robert Babuška
abstract: System identification requires expert decisions on the identification method, incorporation of prior physical knowledge, and model validation. authors: Zheng Jiang, Fang Niu, Bo Peng et al.
abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems rather than as a standalone model operating within a single context. authors: Tingcheng Bian, Kangye Gong, Jinchang Luo et al.

authors: Pekka Abrahamsson, Muhammad Waseem, Esa Karjalainen et al.
abstract: Coordination between large language-model agents has become a central question for AI safety and software engineering, as such agents are deployed in groups that share infrastructure. authors: Shiqi Chen, Daniel Madrigal Diaz, Wei-Ning Chen et al.
